title: Rosuvastatin
disclaimer: Educational summary of public regulatory and scientific sources (Spanish and EU product information and assessment reports, clinical trial registers, ESC/EAS guidelines), current as of the Crestor 5/10/20 mg SmPC revised in October 2025. This is not medical advice and not promotional material. Treatment decisions must follow the current official product information and a qualified healthcare professional.

## What rosuvastatin is

Rosuvastatin is a **statin**, one of a family of medicines that lower cholesterol by slowing how much of it the liver makes. It is taken as one tablet a day, at any time of day, with or without food.

This module is built on one document: the **SmPC** (summary of product characteristics, the regulator-approved reference text for prescribers) for Crestor 5, 10 and 20 mg, as authorised in Spain, where the marketing authorisation holder is Grünenthal GmbH. The version used is the text revised in **October 2025**. Wherever another source disagrees about what is approved, the SmPC wins.

## What it is approved for

The SmPC lists three uses:

- High cholesterol in adults, and in children from 6 years old. This covers raised **LDL cholesterol** (the fraction most closely tied to artery disease), including **familial hypercholesterolaemia** (an inherited form that raises LDL from birth), and **mixed dyslipidaemia** (raised cholesterol and triglycerides together). In each case it is added to diet when diet and other non-drug measures haven't been enough.
- The rare form in which both parents passed on the gene (homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia), from 6 years old, alongside diet and other lipid treatments such as LDL apheresis, a dialysis-like filtering of LDL out of the blood.
- Prevention of major cardiovascular events in people at high risk of a *first* event, alongside correcting their other risk factors.

## What it does to blood fats

The SmPC's dose table comes from a small study with 17 or 18 people per dose and 13 on **placebo** (a dummy tablet). LDL cholesterol fell by 45% at 5 mg, 52% at 10 mg, 55% at 20 mg and 63% at 40 mg, compared with 7% on placebo.

Two cautions apply. First, the table doesn't state how long people were treated, which is part of the time point every number needs. The SmPC says separately that the effect starts within a week and reaches its maximum by about four weeks. Second, the groups are tiny, so treat the exact figures as orientation.

The **comparator** here, meaning the treatment the medicine is measured against, is placebo.

## What it does to heart attacks and strokes

The prevention indication rests on JUPITER, a trial of 17,802 people who took rosuvastatin 20 mg or placebo for a mean of two years. In it, LDL was 45% lower on rosuvastatin than on placebo.

Notice how the SmPC tells the rest of the story. It doesn't give the trial's overall result. Instead it describes two **post-hoc analyses** (analyses chosen after the data had been seen) of higher-risk participants, both showing fewer cardiovascular deaths, strokes and heart attacks. In neither analysis was death from any cause reduced.

Lesson 8 shows the full trial.

## What to watch

- Muscles: aches are common, while **rhabdomyolysis** (severe muscle breakdown that can damage the kidneys) is rare. Reports rise at 40 mg.
- The liver: **transaminases** (liver enzymes measured in a blood test) should be checked before starting treatment and again three months later.
- The kidneys: at high doses, some people develop **proteinuria** (protein in the urine). It's usually temporary.
- Blood sugar: in JUPITER, 2.8% of people on rosuvastatin developed diabetes, compared with 2.3% on placebo.

Rosuvastatin must not be used in:

- active liver disease
- severe kidney impairment
- existing muscle disease
- people taking ciclosporin
- pregnancy or breastfeeding, or women who could become pregnant and aren't using adequate contraception

Lessons 11 and 12 cover each of these.

## What this module is, and isn't

This is a learning module, not prescribing advice. Every lesson is dated to the SmPC revision above. The module is refreshed every six months, or straight away if the SmPC changes or a **safety signal** (new evidence suggesting a possible side effect) appears.

One point to note from the start: this Spanish SmPC covers 5, 10 and 20 mg tablets, yet it still contains dosing rules for 40 mg. Lesson 5 explains why.

## The enzyme it blocks

Rosuvastatin blocks **HMG-CoA reductase**, the liver enzyme that controls the **rate-limiting step** in making cholesterol, meaning the slowest step, which sets the pace for the whole process. The enzyme turns a molecule called HMG-CoA into mevalonate, an early building block of cholesterol. Rosuvastatin competes with HMG-CoA for the enzyme's active site, and it acts mainly in the liver, the organ it is designed to reach.

## Why LDL falls

When the liver makes less cholesterol, it compensates by putting more **LDL receptors** on its surface. These are docking points that pull LDL particles out of the blood. More receptors means more LDL is cleared.

The liver also makes less **VLDL** (very-low-density lipoprotein, the particle that carries triglycerides and later becomes LDL). Fewer VLDL particles today means fewer LDL particles tomorrow.

## Reading that table honestly

Triglycerides fell by 35% at 5 mg but only 10% at 10 mg. A medicine doesn't usually work less well at a higher dose, and nothing in the SmPC suggests rosuvastatin does. With 17 people per group, one or two unusual results can move the average a long way. Small groups make noisy numbers, and noisy numbers deserve light weight.

## Beyond LDL

The SmPC reports that rosuvastatin also lowers **apolipoprotein B**, the protein that sits on every artery-clogging particle, one per particle. It lowers **non-HDL cholesterol** (total cholesterol minus HDL) and raises apolipoprotein A1, the main protein on HDL.

All of these are **markers**, things measured in the blood. They show what the medicine does to lipids, not what it does for the patient.

## What happens in the body

Blood levels peak about five hours after a dose. Only around 20% of a dose reaches the circulation, which is its **bioavailability**. About 90% of the rosuvastatin in the blood is bound to proteins, mainly albumin.

Only about 10% is broken down, mostly by the liver enzyme CYP2C9. Around 90% leaves the body unchanged in the faeces. Its **half-life**, the time it takes for blood levels to fall by half, is about 19 hours.

The Dutch assessment report gives protein binding as about 85% rather than 90%. The difference is small, but it's a reminder that source documents don't always agree.

## Transporters, not metabolism

Most of rosuvastatin's interactions don't come from liver enzymes. They come from **transporter proteins**, which move medicines into and out of cells. OATP1B1 pulls rosuvastatin into liver cells, and BCRP pumps it out of cells. Blocking either one raises blood levels.

Exposure is measured as **AUC** (area under the curve, the total amount in the blood over time). Ciclosporin, for example, raises rosuvastatin's AUC about 7 times, which is why the combination is contraindicated.

Inherited differences in the genes for these transporters also matter. A **genetic variant** that weakens OATP1B1 (SLCO1B1 c.521CC) raises exposure about 1.6 times; one that weakens BCRP (ABCG2 c.421AA) raises it about 2.4 times. For people known to carry either variant, the SmPC advises half the usual dose and a maximum of 20 mg.

## Why ancestry appears in the label

Pharmacokinetic studies show about twice the exposure in Japanese, Chinese, Vietnamese and Korean patients, and about 1.3 times in Indo-Asian patients, compared with white patients. The SmPC therefore recommends a starting dose of 5 mg for patients of Asian origin and contraindicates the 40 mg dose in them.

## A late arrival

Rosuvastatin was discovered by the Japanese company Shionogi. It is fully synthetic, unlike the earliest statins, which came from fungi. AstraZeneca licensed the worldwide rights from Shionogi and developed the medicine under the code ZD4522, which is still engraved on every Crestor tablet.

By the time it reached patients, several other statins were already established. It had to earn its place against them.

## A contested European start

The first approval came in the Netherlands on 6 November 2002. The Netherlands then acted as the **reference member state**, the country that assesses a medicine first on behalf of the others, in a **mutual recognition procedure**, in which other EU countries are asked to accept that first approval.

Twelve countries accepted it by March 2003. Nine countries raised potential serious concerns: about the starting dose, the balance of benefit and risk at 40 mg, use in kidney and liver disease, and interactions. The applications were withdrawn in Germany, Norway and Spain, and France withdrew only the 40 mg strength because of kidney effects. An 80 mg dose had already been dropped, after protein appeared in the urine at 40 and 80 mg.

## The 5 mg question

When a 5 mg tablet was added in 2004, member states disagreed about whether 5 mg should be the starting dose for everyone. The UK sent the question to an **Article 29 referral**, the EU's arbitration route when countries disagree during mutual recognition.

In April 2005 the CHMP, the EMA's main committee for human medicines, concluded that either 5 mg or 10 mg was an acceptable starting dose, chosen according to the patient's cholesterol level and risk factors. The European Commission made that binding in August 2005, and it's still the wording in today's SmPC.

## Early safety scrutiny

In 2004 a US consumer group argued in *The Lancet* that rosuvastatin should be withdrawn, citing reports of kidney failure and rhabdomyolysis. It also pointed to muscle problems in the US pre-approval data at 80 mg, the dose that was later dropped.

The Dutch assessors took a different view of the marketed doses. Muscle findings up to 40 mg were comparable with other statins. In later population studies, rhabdomyolysis occurred at 0.1 per 1,000 patient-years on rosuvastatin versus 0.06 on other statins, a difference that wasn't statistically significant. Their answer was to restrict 40 mg rather than remove it.

## Outcomes came later

When rosuvastatin was first approved there were no data on heart attacks or deaths. Regulators accepted LDL as a **surrogate endpoint**, a lab measure trusted to stand in for clinical outcomes, as they had for other statins.

The outcome trials that followed gave mixed results:

- In chronic heart failure (CORONA), rosuvastatin 10 mg didn't reduce cardiovascular events or deaths.
- In METEOR, it slowed thickening of the neck arteries. That result was added to the label's trial descriptions, but no indication was granted for it.
- JUPITER led to the prevention indication, approved in March 2010. That same month, use in children aged 10–17 was approved; it has since been extended to children from 6.

## Spain joined late

Spain had withdrawn in 2003, so Crestor only arrived there through a later 'repeat-use' procedure, alongside Germany, Malta, Norway and Poland. The Spanish authorisations date from 11 November 2008 (10 and 20 mg) and 15 January 2009 (5 mg). The marketing authorisation holder in Spain is now Grünenthal GmbH.

## One condition behind every use

Each use in the SmPC comes with the same condition: rosuvastatin is an **adjunct**, something added on top of other measures. For high cholesterol, that means diet and other non-drug measures such as exercise and weight loss, which continue during treatment.

The SmPC also asks for **secondary hypercholesterolaemia**, raised cholesterol caused by another condition, to be treated first. It names an underactive thyroid and nephrotic syndrome, a kidney disorder in which protein leaks into the urine.

## Use 1: high cholesterol

The first indication covers primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia. The SmPC names them with the **Fredrickson types**, an older lab classification of lipid disorders: type IIa is raised LDL, and type IIb is raised LDL and triglycerides together. Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia is included.

It applies to adults and to children from 6 years old, in each case only after diet and other measures have not been enough. Children must be treated by specialists. Doses are 5–10 mg from age 6 to 9, and 5–20 mg from age 10 to 17.

## Use 2: the inherited double-copy form

The second indication is homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, from 6 years old. Rosuvastatin is used here alongside diet and other lipid treatments, such as LDL apheresis, or on its own if those treatments aren't appropriate.

The evidence behind this use is thin. The SmPC describes an open-label study of 42 patients (8 of them children) on 20–40 mg, in which LDL fell by an average of 22%. There was no comparator. With a condition this rare, that is often the best evidence available.

## Use 3: preventing a first event

The third indication is **primary prevention**, treatment given before any heart attack or stroke has happened. It covers people at high risk of a *first* major cardiovascular event, alongside correcting their other risk factors, such as blood pressure and smoking. The dose is 20 mg, the dose used in JUPITER.

For who counts as high risk, the indication points to section 5.1. That section describes JUPITER's post-hoc analyses of higher-risk participants, so the indication's boundaries are drawn from them.

## Notice what isn't there

Three uses were proposed or tested but aren't in the label:

- Raised triglycerides on their own. Regulators called this 'a poorly defined entity' and didn't accept it as an indication.
- Slowing the build-up of plaque in the arteries. The METEOR trial is described in the label, but no indication was granted.
- Heart failure. The CORONA trial didn't show a benefit.

There is also no separate prevention indication for people who have already had a heart attack or stroke. The prevention wording is about a first event only.

## The US door is wider in some places

The US label includes three indications the EU never granted: raised triglycerides, primary dysbetalipoproteinaemia (a rare inherited lipid disorder), and slowing the progression of atherosclerosis, the plaque build-up that METEOR measured. Its prevention wording also covers 'adults at increased risk' without limiting it to a first event.

In two places it is narrower: for children, it starts at age 8 in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia and at 7 in the homozygous form, while the EU label starts at 6 for both.

## The tablets this module is built on

Crestor comes as round **film-coated tablets** (tablets with a thin outer layer). The 5 mg tablet is yellow, and the 10 mg and 20 mg tablets are pink. Every tablet is engraved 'ZD4522' plus its strength, which is the development code from Lesson 3.

The most important **excipient** (an ingredient other than the active substance) for patients is lactose, from about 91 mg per tablet at 10 mg to about 183 mg at 20 mg. Crestor comes in blister packs of 7 to 100 tablets, or in bottles of 30 or 100. It keeps for three years below 30 °C, in the original pack to protect it from moisture.

## Who stands behind it

In Spain, the **MAH** (marketing authorisation holder, the company legally responsible for the product) is now Grünenthal GmbH, of Aachen, Germany. The tablets are made by Grünenthal and by Farmaceutici Formenti in Italy, and Almirall is the local representative.

According to the PIL, the same product is sold as Crestor in 17 countries of the European Economic Area, from the Netherlands and Germany to Portugal and Poland.

## The 40 mg question

The Crestor SmPC on CIMA lists only 5, 10 and 20 mg, yet it contains rules for 40 mg. The PIL even describes stepping the dose up to 40 mg.

The reason is that 40 mg rosuvastatin *is* part of the Spanish market. Generic 40 mg tablets are authorised in Spain, and the Spanish agency's 2015 assessment reports name Crestor 40 mg as their reference product. The SmPC text also comes from the shared EU procedure, which always included 40 mg.

This module couldn't confirm whether a separate Crestor 40 mg listing is still active. The practical point stands, though: the 40 mg rules apply to every rosuvastatin 40 mg tablet a patient might receive.

## Generics

Many **generics** (copies authorised because they match the original) are sold in Spain, with the letters EFG on the pack. Some differ from Crestor in small but useful ways. Several have a score line and can be split into equal halves, whereas Crestor is swallowed whole.

Several companies, including Krka, Normon, Teva and Cinfa, also sell 15 mg and 30 mg tablets. Crestor was never made in those strengths, so they aren't labelled as generics.

## Combination products in Spain

Rosuvastatin is also sold combined with other medicines in one tablet or capsule:

- with ezetimibe: many companies, 5 to 40 mg rosuvastatin with 10 mg ezetimibe
- with fenofibrate: several companies, including Tecnimede, Intas, Viatris and Althera (see the fenofibrate module)
- with amlodipine, a blood pressure medicine: capsules of 10 or 20 mg rosuvastatin with 5 or 10 mg amlodipine
- with valsartan, a blood pressure medicine (Valsaros): 10 or 20 mg rosuvastatin with 80 or 160 mg valsartan
- with acetylsalicylic acid (Roasax): capsules of 5, 10 or 20 mg rosuvastatin with 100 mg aspirin

The ones checked for this module are for **substitution therapy** only, meaning they replace the same medicines already being taken separately at the same doses. Lesson 9 goes through the evidence behind each pairing.

## The routine

Rosuvastatin is taken once a day, at any time of day, with or without food. The tablet is swallowed whole with water. The PIL suggests taking it at the same time every day, because that makes it easier to remember.

Diet and exercise continue alongside the tablet.

## Starting and adjusting

For high cholesterol, treatment starts at 5 mg or 10 mg, even for someone switching from a higher dose of another statin. The choice depends on the person's cholesterol level, their cardiovascular risk and their risk of side effects. After four weeks the dose can go up one step.

40 mg is reserved for severe high cholesterol at high cardiovascular risk (especially familial hypercholesterolaemia) that isn't at goal on 20 mg. It requires routine follow-up and should be started under specialist supervision.

For the prevention indication, the dose is 20 mg.

## Who starts at 5 mg

The SmPC recommends starting at 5 mg for:

- people over 70
- people of Asian origin
- moderate kidney impairment
- factors that predispose to muscle problems
- other medicines that at least double rosuvastatin exposure

People known to carry one of the transporter gene variants from Lesson 2 take half the usual dose, with a maximum of 20 mg.

One small mismatch: the PIL's list of Asian origins includes Filipino, while the SmPC's pharmacokinetic section names Japanese, Chinese, Vietnamese, Korean and Indo-Asian patients.

## Kidneys and liver

Kidney function is measured here as **creatinine clearance**, how much blood the kidneys clean of creatinine each minute.

- Below 30 mL/min: rosuvastatin must not be used.
- Below 60 mL/min: start at 5 mg; 40 mg is contraindicated.

Liver function is graded with the **Child-Pugh score**, which rates how severe liver disease is.

- Score 7 or below: exposure doesn't rise.
- Score 8–9: exposure rises, and kidney function should be assessed.
- Above 9: there is no experience.
- Active liver disease: rosuvastatin is contraindicated.

## The checks

Liver tests are done before starting treatment and three months later. Treatment is stopped, or the dose reduced, if transaminases rise above three times the **ULN** (upper limit of normal, the top of the laboratory's reference range).

Muscle is tracked with **CK** (creatine kinase, a muscle enzyme measured in the blood). Routine CK checks aren't needed in people without symptoms, and CK shouldn't be measured after strenuous exercise. If it's above five times the ULN before treatment, the test is repeated within 5–7 days, and treatment isn't started if the result is confirmed.

## Missed doses and stopping

If a dose is missed, the PIL says simply to take the next one at the usual time, without doubling up. Anyone who wants to stop should talk to their doctor first, because cholesterol levels rise again once treatment ends.

## Pregnancy, breastfeeding and children

Rosuvastatin is contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Women who could become pregnant need adequate contraception, and treatment must stop immediately if a pregnancy occurs.

Children are treated only by specialists. It isn't recommended under 6.

## Overdose

There is no specific treatment for an overdose. Care is supportive, with liver function and CK monitored, and haemodialysis is unlikely to help. In Spain, the PIL gives the national toxicology information line.

## Why this lesson comes first

The next two lessons are built from trials. Each trial appears on the same card, so you can read them all the same way. This lesson covers the ideas those cards rely on, using rosuvastatin's own trials as the examples.

## Who gets what

Many trials begin with a **run-in**, a short lead-in period on a fixed treatment. It shows who tolerates the treatment and who keeps taking it. JUPITER used a four-week run-in on placebo tablets, so only people who took their tablets reliably went on to be randomised.

After the run-in, a **double-blind** design keeps both participants and investigators unaware of who is getting what, so expectations can't tilt the results.

## What counts as the answer

Each trial names its **primary endpoint** in advance: the single measure that decides whether the trial succeeded. Outcome trials often use a **composite endpoint**, which counts several kinds of event together.

Composites can differ a lot between trials. JUPITER's included hospitalisation for unstable angina and artery-opening procedures, as well as heart attack, stroke and cardiovascular death. HOPE-3's first primary endpoint counted only the last three. Before comparing results, check what was counted.

## Two ways to state the same effect

In HOPE-3, over a median of 5.6 years, 4.8% of people on placebo and 3.7% on rosuvastatin had a cardiovascular death, heart attack or stroke.

The **absolute risk reduction** is the plain difference between those figures: 1.1 percentage points. The **relative risk reduction** expresses that difference as a share of the placebo figure, which the trial reported as about 24%. The same result sounds small one way and larger the other. That is why this module always gives both, along with what the treatment was compared against and over what time.

## Hazard ratios and confidence intervals

A **hazard ratio** (HR) compares how often events happened with treatment against how often they happened in the comparison group, over the course of the trial. The **confidence interval** (CI) gives the range of values the data are compatible with.

HOPE-3's HR was 0.76, with a CI of 0.64 to 0.91. The whole range sits below 1.0, which means no difference, so the result is statistically significant. CORONA's HR was 0.92, with a CI of 0.83 to 1.02. That range crosses 1.0, so the result is compatible with no effect. The **p-value** says the same thing another way: 0.002 for HOPE-3 and 0.12 for CORONA, against the usual bar of 0.05.

## Rates per person-year

Some trials report events per 100 **person-years**. Person-years add up the time each participant was followed, so 100 people followed for two years count as 200 person-years. This is useful when people are followed for different lengths of time.

JUPITER reported 0.77 events per 100 person-years on rosuvastatin and 1.36 on placebo. That's an absolute difference of about 0.6 per 100 person-years, or about 6 events per 1,000 people per year.

## Turning a result into people

The **number needed to treat** (NNT) is 100 divided by the absolute risk reduction in percentage points. It tells you how many people need treating, for a stated time, to prevent one event.

For HOPE-3's first primary outcome, 100 ÷ 1.1 gives about 91 people treated for 5.6 years to prevent one cardiovascular death, heart attack or stroke. This figure is calculated here from the trial's published numbers.

## When a trial stops early

An independent **data safety monitoring board** looks at results while a trial is still running. If one arm is clearly doing better, the board can stop the trial.

JUPITER was **stopped early for benefit**, after a median of 1.9 years of a planned four or so. Stopping at a moment when the benefit looks large tends to overstate the true effect, and a review of stopped trials in *JAMA* in 2010 found this pattern across medicine. The benefit may be real but smaller than the headline figure.

## Planned before or chosen after

A subgroup analysis that was **prespecified**, written into the plan before any results were seen, carries more weight than a post-hoc analysis chosen afterwards. The strongest subgroup findings also pass a test for **interaction**, which checks whether the effect genuinely differs between subgroups.

This matters for rosuvastatin. The EU label describes JUPITER mainly through post-hoc analyses of higher-risk participants, and those analyses define who counts as high risk for the prevention indication.

## Who is counted

Most outcome trials are analysed by **intention to treat**: everyone stays in the group they were randomised to, whether or not they kept taking the tablets. This protects the comparison. It also means the result reflects the medicine as people actually took it, stops and all.

Some trials test **non-inferiority**, asking whether a new approach is not worse than the standard by more than a limit set in advance. Several rosuvastatin combination trials in Lesson 9 are built this way.

## The combination tags

Each trial card carries exactly one tag. The tag describes the lipid-lowering treatment participants were already on, plus any Lesson 9 partner medicine given or randomised by design. Everyday usual-care medicines taken by some participants don't change it.

- 🔗 +EZE: everyone was on ezetimibe
- 🔗 +EZE+PCSK9: everyone was on ezetimibe and a PCSK9 inhibitor
- 🔗 +EZE+BEMP: everyone was on ezetimibe and bempedoic acid
- 🔗 +ASA: everyone was on acetylsalicylic acid
- 🔗 +SGLT2: everyone was on dapagliflozin or empagliflozin
- 🔗 +ANTIHTN: everyone was on a listed blood-pressure medicine, taken as a separate tablet
- 🔗 FDC: two or more medicines in one tablet or capsule
- 🔗 MIXED: only part of the trial received a Lesson 9 partner by design
- STATIN-INTOLERANT: participants couldn't take a statin
- MONO: no lipid-lowering background and no Lesson 9 partner

**Ezetimibe** is a cholesterol medicine that reduces how much cholesterol the gut absorbs.

## Reading a card

Every card has the same eight lines:

- registry number
- who took part
- background therapy
- what it was compared with
- the main question
- the headline result
- in plain words
- what's worth knowing

The **registry number** points to the trial's public record, where its plan was written down before the results came in.

## Five trials, three kinds of answer

A **pivotal trial** is one that regulators or clinical practice rely on. Rosuvastatin's large outcome trials fall into three groups:

- two positive trials in people without heart disease: JUPITER and HOPE-3
- one imaging trial measuring a marker: METEOR
- two neutral trials in people with advanced disease: CORONA in heart failure and AURORA in dialysis

The EU SmPC describes only JUPITER and METEOR. The cards below show all five.

### Trial card: JUPITER
Tag: MONO

- Registry: NCT00239681
- Who took part: 17,802 people without heart disease or diabetes (men aged 50 or over, women 60 or over), with normal LDL (below 3.4 mmol/L) and raised C-reactive protein (2 mg/L or above), an inflammation marker
- Background therapy: none. People on current or previous lipid-lowering treatment were excluded. A four-week placebo run-in selected people who took their tablets reliably.
- Compared with: placebo. Stopped early after a median of 1.9 years (maximum 5.0), of a planned four or so.
- Main question: does rosuvastatin 20 mg reduce first major cardiovascular events (heart attack, stroke, artery-opening procedure, hospitalisation for unstable angina, cardiovascular death)?
- Headline result: 0.77 vs 1.36 events per 100 person-years; 142 vs 251 events; HR 0.56 (95% CI 0.46–0.69). That is about 44% lower in relative terms and about 6 fewer events per 1,000 people per year in absolute terms. Death from any cause: 1.00 vs 1.25 per 100 person-years; HR 0.80 (95% CI 0.67–0.97).
- In plain words: in people with normal LDL but raised inflammation, rosuvastatin cut first cardiovascular events by almost half in relative terms over about two years.
- Worth knowing: early stopping tends to overstate effects. Diabetes was reported more often on rosuvastatin (2.8% vs 2.3% in the SmPC). The EU SmPC doesn't give this overall result; it gives post-hoc higher-risk analyses instead. Even event counts can drift between documents: the US label counts 252 placebo events, the publication 251.

### Trial card: HOPE-3
Tag: 🔗 MIXED

- Registry: NCT00468923
- Who took part: 12,705 people at intermediate risk without cardiovascular disease, from 21 countries and many ethnic backgrounds
- Background therapy: in a **factorial design** (one group of participants randomised to two questions at once), half were also randomised to candesartan 16 mg plus hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg for blood pressure, and half to placebo. Lesson 9 covers that combination.
- Compared with: placebo, over a median of 5.6 years
- Main question: does rosuvastatin 10 mg, at a fixed dose with no lipid targets, reduce cardiovascular death, heart attack or stroke?
- Headline result: 3.7% vs 4.8%; HR 0.76 (95% CI 0.64–0.91), p = 0.002. That is about 24% lower in relative terms and 1.1 percentage points lower in absolute terms over 5.6 years. The broader second primary outcome was 4.4% vs 5.7% (HR 0.75).
- In plain words: a moderate fixed dose lowered events in people who weren't high risk and didn't have high cholesterol.
- Worth knowing: LDL was on average 26.5% lower than on placebo over the trial. That is about half the fall in the SmPC's short dose table, but they are different studies in different people over different times, so don't compare them head-to-head. Muscle symptoms were more frequent (5.8% vs 4.7%), and so was cataract surgery. HOPE-3 doesn't appear in the EU SmPC.

### Trial card: METEOR
Tag: MONO

- Registry: NCT00225589
- Who took part: 984 people aged 45–70 at low coronary risk (below 10% over 10 years), with an average LDL of 4.0 mmol/L and early, silent artery disease
- Background therapy: none
- Compared with: placebo, over 2 years; rosuvastatin 40 mg
- Main question: does rosuvastatin slow the thickening of the neck artery wall, measured by ultrasound as **CIMT** (carotid intima-media thickness)?
- Headline result: CIMT progressed 0.0145 mm per year less than on placebo (95% CI 0.0093–0.0196). It barely changed on rosuvastatin (−0.0014 mm per year, not significant) and increased on placebo (+0.0131 mm per year).
- In plain words: over two years, the artery wall stopped thickening on rosuvastatin and kept thickening on placebo.
- Worth knowing: CIMT is a surrogate endpoint. The SmPC says outright that no direct link between reduced CIMT and fewer events has been shown, and that these low-risk people aren't the target population for 40 mg. No indication was granted.

### Trial card: CORONA
Tag: MONO

- Registry: NCT00206310
- Who took part: 5,011 people aged 60 or over with ischaemic systolic heart failure (NYHA class II–IV) who didn't need cholesterol treatment
- Background therapy: optimal heart-failure treatment; no lipid-lowering treatment
- Compared with: placebo, over a median of 32.8 months; rosuvastatin 10 mg
- Main question: does rosuvastatin reduce cardiovascular death, heart attack or stroke?
- Headline result: 692 vs 732 events; HR 0.92 (95% CI 0.83–1.02), p = 0.12. Deaths: 728 vs 759 (HR 0.95). Not statistically significant.
- In plain words: LDL fell 45%, but the main outcome and deaths didn't change significantly.
- Worth knowing: a prespecified secondary analysis found fewer cardiovascular hospitalisations (2,193 vs 2,564). There were no muscle safety problems. The Dutch assessors noted the trial didn't alter the safety profile. No heart-failure indication exists.

## A second heart-failure trial

GISSI-HF randomised 4,574 people with heart failure to rosuvastatin 10 mg or placebo for 3.9 years. The hazard ratio for death was 1.00 (95% CI 0.90–1.12). Two heart-failure trials together found no effect on death. This trial has no card because its registry record wasn't checked in this pass.

### Trial card: AURORA
Tag: MONO

- Registry: NCT00240331
- Who took part: 2,776 people aged 50–80 on maintenance haemodialysis, not already on a statin
- Background therapy: usual dialysis care; no lipid-lowering treatment
- Compared with: placebo, over a median of 3.8 years; rosuvastatin 10 mg
- Main question: does rosuvastatin reduce cardiovascular death, heart attack or stroke?
- Headline result: 9.2 vs 9.5 events per 100 person-years; HR 0.96 (95% CI 0.84–1.11), p = 0.59. Death from any cause: 13.5 vs 14.0 per 100 person-years (HR 0.96).
- In plain words: LDL fell 43% at three months, but cardiovascular events didn't change.
- Worth knowing: the EU SmPC contraindicates rosuvastatin in severe kidney impairment, which includes people on dialysis. The US label allows 5–10 mg in severe impairment when the person isn't on dialysis. AURORA isn't mentioned in the SmPC.

The columns come from different trials in different people, so read each one on its own and don't compare across them. Taken separately, the pattern is clear. Rosuvastatin reduced events in people without established disease. In heart failure and in dialysis, lowering LDL wasn't enough to change outcomes.

## Two kinds of partner

Rosuvastatin is rarely a person's only heart medicine. This lesson covers two kinds of partner. Part A covers other lipid medicines: ezetimibe, and, on top of that, a PCSK9 inhibitor or bempedoic acid. Part B covers cardiometabolic medicines: acetylsalicylic acid, the SGLT2 inhibitors dapagliflozin and empagliflozin, and seven blood-pressure medicines (telmisartan, valsartan, losartan, amlodipine, lercanidipine, hydrochlorothiazide and indapamide).

For each partner, the lesson asks three questions. What do the licences actually name? What does the Crestor SmPC say about the pairing? And what trials exist?

## What the licences name

A **fixed-dose combination** puts two or more medicines in one tablet or capsule. The following were found in Spain or elsewhere in the EU:

- Crestor itself names no partner. Section 5.1 mentions only small studies with fenofibrate and niacin.
- Rosuvastatin + ezetimibe (many Spanish products): substitution, for primary hypercholesterolaemia. Some also cover coronary heart disease after an acute coronary syndrome.
- Rosuvastatin + fenofibrate (Spain): substitution (see the fenofibrate module).
- Rosuvastatin + amlodipine (Spain): substitution, for people already controlled on both medicines taken separately.
- Rosuvastatin + valsartan (Valsaros) and rosuvastatin + acetylsalicylic acid (Roasax): authorised in Spain. Their indication text wasn't reviewed in this pass.
- Rosuvastatin + perindopril + indapamide (Roxiper): authorised through a **decentralised procedure** (several EU countries assessing one application together, here led by Hungary) for high blood pressure with high cholesterol, as substitution. It is contraindicated when creatinine clearance is below 60.

## What no licence names

This pass found no EU licence that combines rosuvastatin with telmisartan, losartan, lercanidipine, hydrochlorothiazide, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, a PCSK9 inhibitor or bempedoic acid.

When these medicines are combined in practice, each is prescribed on its own licence, taken as a separate tablet. That is **co-administration**: taking two medicines together without a combined product.

## The Crestor SmPC's interaction lines

For lipid partners:

- Ezetimibe raises rosuvastatin exposure about 1.2-fold. An interaction on side effects can't be ruled out, and very rare rhabdomyolysis has been reported with ezetimibe plus statins, so the SmPC asks for caution.
- Fenofibrate has no meaningful effect on blood levels, but the muscle risk may add up. 40 mg is contraindicated with any fibrate, and treatment starts at 5 mg.
- Gemfibrozil almost doubles exposure (×1.9) and isn't recommended.

For antiplatelet partners, often taken alongside aspirin: clopidogrel doubles exposure, and ticagrelor raises it 2.6-fold.

The SmPC has no line at all for acetylsalicylic acid, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, any of the seven blood-pressure medicines, PCSK9 inhibitors or bempedoic acid.

## How to read those columns

Read each column on its own. They come from different trials, in different people, over different time frames. The table shows how much evidence exists for each approach, not which one works best. No trial has compared all three head-to-head.

### Trial card: RACING
Tag: 🔗 MIXED

- Registry: NCT03044665
- Who took part: 3,780 people with established atherosclerotic disease at 26 centres in South Korea; average LDL about 80 mg/dL at entry
- Background therapy: half were randomised to add ezetimibe; the trial allowed doses to be adjusted to reach the LDL target
- Compared with: rosuvastatin 20 mg alone. Open-label (everyone knew which treatment they were on). Non-inferiority margin of 2.0 percentage points. 3 years.
- Main question: is rosuvastatin 10 mg plus ezetimibe 10 mg no worse than rosuvastatin 20 mg at preventing cardiovascular death, major cardiovascular events or stroke?
- Headline result: 9.1% vs 9.9% at 3 years; difference −0.78 percentage points (90% CI −2.39 to 0.83). That is about 8% lower in relative terms (calculated here), and within the non-inferiority margin.
- In plain words: adding ezetimibe to a moderate dose was no worse than doubling the statin.
- Worth knowing: fewer people stopped or reduced treatment on the combination. Korean patients carry about twice the rosuvastatin exposure of white patients (Lesson 2), so the doses don't translate one-to-one to European patients. Being open-label, it's weaker than a blinded trial for softer outcomes.

### Trial card: HOPE-3, combined arm
Tag: 🔗 MIXED

- Registry: NCT00468923
- Who took part: 6,348 people at intermediate risk without cardiovascular disease, from HOPE-3's factorial design
- Background therapy: none. This comparison takes the two extreme arms of the factorial design.
- Compared with: dual placebo (3,168 people) versus rosuvastatin 10 mg plus candesartan 16 mg plus hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg (3,180 people), over a median of 5.6 years
- Main question: does lowering cholesterol and blood pressure together reduce cardiovascular death, heart attack or stroke?
- Headline result: 3.6% vs 5.0%; HR 0.71 (95% CI 0.56–0.90), p = 0.005. That is about 29% lower in relative terms and 1.4 percentage points lower in absolute terms over 5.6 years. LDL was 0.87 mmol/L lower and systolic blood pressure 6.2 mmHg lower.
- In plain words: rosuvastatin plus two blood-pressure medicines lowered events more clearly than either approach showed on its own.
- Worth knowing: muscle weakness and dizziness were more common, but about as many people stopped treatment in each arm. The medicines were given as separate tablets, not as a single pill. Hydrochlorothiazide is on this lesson's list; candesartan isn't. No EU licence names this combination.

### Trial card: telmisartan/amlodipine plus rosuvastatin
Tag: 🔗 +ANTIHTN

- Registry: NCT03067688
- Who took part: 202 Korean patients with high blood pressure and high cholesterol
- Background therapy: telmisartan 80 mg in every arm
- Compared with: telmisartan 80 mg plus rosuvastatin 20 mg, and telmisartan/amlodipine 80/5 mg, over 8 weeks
- Main question: does telmisartan/amlodipine plus rosuvastatin lower blood pressure more than telmisartan plus rosuvastatin, and LDL more than telmisartan/amlodipine?
- Headline result: systolic blood pressure fell by 19.3 vs 6.7 mmHg at 8 weeks, a difference of −12.6 mmHg (95% CI −18.1 to −7.1). LDL fell 52.5% with the three medicines and rose 2.7% on telmisartan/amlodipine alone, a difference of −55.1 percentage points (95% CI −61.5 to −48.8).
- In plain words: adding amlodipine lowered blood pressure further, and rosuvastatin didn't get in the way.
- Worth knowing: no adverse events led to stopping treatment. This is an 8-week trial measuring markers only, with no outcome data. A second, smaller Korean trial of the same combination (NCT03566316, 134 people) was published in 2019. Telmisartan and rosuvastatin aren't combined in any EU licence found in this pass.

### Trial card: amlodipine/rosuvastatin single pill
Tag: 🔗 FDC

- Registry: not found in this search
- Who took part: 106 Korean patients with high blood pressure and high cholesterol, at 15 centres
- Background therapy: none; 4-week placebo run-in with lifestyle measures
- Compared with: amlodipine 10 mg alone, and rosuvastatin 20 mg alone, over 8 weeks
- Main question: does one pill of rosuvastatin 20 mg plus amlodipine 10 mg lower blood pressure and LDL like its parts?
- Headline result: systolic blood pressure fell by 22.8 mmHg in the single-pill group, the largest fall of the three arms. The between-group LDL figures weren't extracted in this pass.
- In plain words: the single pill did both jobs over 8 weeks.
- Worth knowing: the trial is small and short. Rosuvastatin + amlodipine is licensed in Spain as capsules, for substitution only.

### Trial card: ezetimibe/rosuvastatin plus telmisartan
Tag: 🔗 MIXED

- Registry: not found in this search
- Who took part: 181 South Korean patients with high cholesterol and high blood pressure
- Background therapy: ezetimibe/rosuvastatin in two of the three arms
- Compared with: ezetimibe/rosuvastatin 10/20 mg alone, and telmisartan 80 mg alone, over 8 weeks
- Main question: do all three medicines together lower blood pressure and LDL as well as their parts?
- Headline result: systolic blood pressure fell by 25.8 vs 7.7 mmHg (all three vs ezetimibe/rosuvastatin alone) at 8 weeks. The LDL figures weren't extracted in this pass.
- In plain words: adding telmisartan lowered blood pressure without affecting the lipid treatment.
- Worth knowing: one of the few trials combining rosuvastatin, ezetimibe and a blood-pressure medicine. It measured markers only.

The evidence divides into two very different kinds. On the lipid side there are outcome trials (JUPITER, HOPE-3, RACING). A **polypill**, a single pill combining several heart medicines, has outcome evidence in general. The one rosuvastatin-plus-aspirin polypill trial found here, a 140-person phase 2 study, has posted results that haven't yet been reviewed for this module.

## The question that matters

Lower LDL is a marker. This lesson asks what patients care about: does rosuvastatin mean fewer heart attacks, strokes and deaths?

The EU SmPC answers through JUPITER's post-hoc higher-risk analyses. In those, rosuvastatin reduced a combination of cardiovascular death, stroke and heart attack. Death from any cause was not affected in either analysis.

## Heart attacks and strokes in JUPITER

Across the whole trial (rosuvastatin 20 mg vs placebo, median 1.9 years):

- **Heart attack:** 0.17 vs 0.37 per 100 person-years (HR 0.46). That is about 54% lower in relative terms, and about 2 fewer per 1,000 people per year.
- **Stroke:** 0.18 vs 0.34 per 100 person-years (HR 0.52). That is about 48% lower in relative terms, and about 1.6 fewer per 1,000 people per year.

Remember that JUPITER stopped early (Lesson 7). The true effects may be somewhat smaller than these figures.

## Death: two sources, two framings

JUPITER's publication reports fewer deaths from any cause across the whole trial: 1.00 vs 1.25 per 100 person-years (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.67–0.97).

The EU SmPC doesn't report that overall figure. It reports only the higher-risk post-hoc analyses, and in both of them death from any cause wasn't significantly reduced (p = 0.193 and p = 0.076). Both statements are accurate. They describe different slices of the same trial.

In advanced disease, rosuvastatin didn't reduce deaths: CORONA (HR 0.95), AURORA (HR 0.96) and GISSI-HF (HR 1.00).

### Trial card: LODESTAR
Tag: MONO

- Registry: NCT02579499
- Who took part: 4,400 adults with coronary artery disease at 12 hospitals in South Korea
- Background therapy: no lipid partner. A factorial design also randomised how the dose was chosen, but not any partner medicine.
- Compared with: atorvastatin, open-label, over 3 years. Average doses were 17.1 mg rosuvastatin and 36.0 mg atorvastatin.
- Main question: does rosuvastatin do better than atorvastatin on death, heart attack, stroke or coronary revascularisation?
- Headline result: 8.7% vs 8.2%; HR 1.06 (95% CI 0.86–1.30), p = 0.58. That is 0.5 percentage points higher on rosuvastatin, which isn't statistically significant.
- In plain words: in a **head-to-head trial**, which directly compares two active treatments, the two statins performed about the same on hard outcomes, even though LDL ran slightly lower on rosuvastatin (1.8 vs 1.9 mmol/L).
- Worth knowing: more new diabetes needing medication (7.2% vs 5.3%) and more cataract surgery (2.5% vs 1.5%) on rosuvastatin (Lesson 11). This was a single-country, open-label trial in Korea, where rosuvastatin exposure runs higher.

## The class picture

The Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' Collaboration pooled 26 statin trials with about 170,000 participants. For every 1.0 mmol/L reduction in LDL, major vascular events fell by about 22% (rate ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.76–0.80) and deaths from any cause by about 10% (rate ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.87–0.93).

These figures are relative and describe statins as a class. The absolute benefit for any one person depends on how high their risk is to start with. So the pooled estimate supports rosuvastatin's direction of effect, but it doesn't give its size for a particular patient.

## How the SmPC counts

The SmPC groups each adverse reaction by how often it occurs:

- common: 1 in 100 to 1 in 10
- uncommon: 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 100
- rare: 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 1,000
- very rare: below 1 in 10,000
- not known: frequency can't be estimated

The SmPC describes side effects as generally mild and short-lived, and fewer than 4% of patients in controlled trials stopped treatment because of them. Like other statins, their frequency tends to rise with the dose.

## Common

- Headache and dizziness
- Constipation, nausea and abdominal pain
- Muscle aches (myalgia)
- Weakness (asthenia)
- Diabetes. How often it appears depends on risk factors: fasting glucose of 5.6 mmol/L or above, BMI above 30, raised triglycerides or high blood pressure.

## Less common, rare and very rare

- Uncommon: itching, rash and hives.
- Rare: low platelets, allergic reactions including angioedema, pancreatitis, raised liver enzymes, myopathy (including inflammation of the muscles), rhabdomyolysis, a lupus-like syndrome and muscle rupture.
- Very rare: nerve damage in the arms and legs, memory loss, jaundice, hepatitis, joint pain, blood in the urine and breast enlargement in men.

## Frequency not known

The SmPC also lists depression, sleep problems, cough and breathlessness, diarrhoea, oedema, tendon problems and anaphylaxis. Several items on this list need their own explanation:

- Severe skin reactions, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and **DRESS** (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms), which can be life-threatening. After either one, rosuvastatin must never be restarted.
- **Immune-mediated necrotising myopathy**: muscle weakness and a raised muscle enzyme that persist even after the statin is stopped.
- New or worsening **myasthenia gravis**, a disease in which muscles weaken with use.

## Kidneys

At higher doses some people develop protein in the urine, mostly of tubular origin, meaning it comes from the kidney's small tubes rather than its filters. A shift to ++ or more was seen in under 1% of people on 10–20 mg and about 3% of people on 40 mg. It usually settles on its own, and it hasn't been shown to predict kidney disease.

Blood in the urine occurs at a low rate. Reports of serious kidney events are more frequent at 40 mg.

## Muscles

Muscle aches are common. Rhabdomyolysis is rare but is reported more often at doses above 20 mg. CK rises with the dose, though mostly mildly and without symptoms. Treatment stops if CK exceeds five times the ULN.

In children, CK above ten times the ULN, and muscle symptoms after exercise, were seen more often than in adults.

In HOPE-3, over 5.6 years, muscle symptoms occurred in 5.8% of people on rosuvastatin 10 mg and 4.7% on placebo, 1.1 percentage points more.

## Reading the diabetes signal

Each column is a separate trial with its own comparator, so don't compare them directly. Diabetes appeared more often with rosuvastatin in JUPITER, and against atorvastatin in LODESTAR, but not in HOPE-3.

The SmPC's position is that the vascular benefit outweighs this risk, and that it shouldn't be a reason to stop a statin. It asks for people at risk of diabetes to be monitored instead.

## A signal the label doesn't carry

LODESTAR found more cataract surgery on rosuvastatin than on atorvastatin (2.5% vs 1.5% over 3 years; HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.07–2.58), and HOPE-3 also reported an excess. Cataract doesn't appear anywhere in the Crestor SmPC.

This is a trial finding that the label hasn't taken up. It isn't proof of harm, but it is worth tracking in Lesson 13.

## When to stop and see a doctor

The PIL tells patients to stop and get help straight away for any of these:

- difficulty breathing, or swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat
- intense itching with hives
- target-shaped skin patches with blisters or mouth ulcers
- a widespread rash with fever and swollen glands
- unexplained muscle pain or cramps that last longer than expected
- a muscle rupture
- lupus-like symptoms

It also asks patients to see a doctor if they notice weakness that gets worse with activity, double vision, drooping eyelids, or difficulty swallowing or breathing. These can be signs of myasthenia.

blocks.markdown:
## Who must not take it, at any dose

- Allergy to rosuvastatin or any ingredient
- Active liver disease, including unexplained persistent rises in transaminases or any rise above three times the ULN
- Severe kidney impairment (creatinine clearance below 30)
- Myopathy
- Taking sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir (a hepatitis C treatment)
- Taking ciclosporin
- Pregnancy or breastfeeding, and women who could become pregnant without adequate contraception

## Who must not take 40 mg

On top of the list above, 40 mg is contraindicated for people with:

- moderate kidney impairment (creatinine clearance below 60)
- an underactive thyroid
- a personal or family history of inherited muscle disorders
- previous muscle problems on a statin or fibrate
- alcohol abuse
- situations that raise blood levels
- Asian origin
- a fibrate being taken at the same time

Each of these factors raises either blood levels or the underlying risk to muscle.

## Extra care, and when not to use it at all

Caution is needed after age 70 and with the muscle risk factors above. Rosuvastatin shouldn't be used at all during an acute, serious illness that could lead to muscle breakdown or kidney failure: sepsis, very low blood pressure, major surgery, trauma, severe metabolic or electrolyte disorders, or uncontrolled seizures.

Other warnings:

- Anyone who has had a severe skin reaction to it must never take it again.
- It can unmask or worsen myasthenia.
- It contains lactose.
- If interstitial lung disease is suspected, treatment must stop.

## A leaflet line without an SmPC twin

The PIL asks patients to talk to their doctor if they have severe respiratory insufficiency. The SmPC's warnings section (October 2025 revision) has no matching line. The nearest it comes is its warning on interstitial lung disease.

PILs are meant to reflect the SmPC. When a line appears only in the PIL, it's worth noting and raising at the next review.

## Medicines that raise exposure

Most interactions work through the transporters from Lesson 2. The SmPC's table lists, among others:

- sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir (×7.4) and ciclosporin (×7.1): contraindicated
- darolutamide (×5.2), regorafenib (×3.8) and atazanavir/ritonavir (×3.1)
- roxadustat (×2.9); velpatasvir, momelotinib and ticagrelor (×2.6–2.7)
- teriflunomide or leflunomide (×2.5), clopidogrel (×2), febuxostat and gemfibrozil (×1.9)

The rule of thumb: if a medicine roughly doubles exposure or more, start at 5 mg, and cap the dose so that total exposure stays at or below 40 mg taken alone. For example, the cap is 20 mg with gemfibrozil, and 10 mg with atazanavir/ritonavir.

## Other interactions

- **Fusidic acid**, an antibiotic: don't combine. Stop rosuvastatin during treatment and for 7 days after, because rhabdomyolysis, including deaths, has been reported with the combination.
- Antacids containing aluminium and magnesium halve rosuvastatin levels. Taking the antacid 2 hours later reduces the effect.
- Erythromycin lowers rosuvastatin exposure by 20%.
- **Vitamin K antagonists** (warfarin-type anticoagulants): starting or raising rosuvastatin can raise the **INR**, a clotting test. Monitor it.
- Oral contraceptives: exposure to ethinylestradiol rises by 26% and to norgestrel by 34%.
- No meaningful interactions through the CYP450 enzymes are expected.

## Watching a medicine after approval

**Pharmacovigilance** is the ongoing monitoring of a medicine's safety once it's on the market. The Crestor SmPC asks healthcare professionals in Spain to report suspected side effects to the national system (notificaRAM.es), and the PIL invites patients to report directly too.

Every statin warning in this module that came after approval started with reports like these.

## The EU's regular check-ups

Companies send a **PSUR** (periodic safety update report) at set intervals. For medicines authorised nationally, the EU assesses all companies' reports on the same substance together in a single **PSUSA** (periodic safety update single assessment).

The most recent rosuvastatin PSUSA found, covering data to November 2022, ended with 'maintenance', meaning no change to the label. Rosuvastatin combinations have their own PSUSAs. Most also ended with maintenance, but at least two ended with a variation, and one of them changed every rosuvastatin label.

## A signal found through a combination product

When the EU reviewed the safety reports for ezetimibe/rosuvastatin (data to July 2020), its safety committee, the **PRAC** (Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee), reached two conclusions:

- Rosuvastatin can cause DRESS. The evidence included cases where symptoms cleared when the medicine was stopped, and one case where they returned when it was restarted.
- Ticagrelor can interact with rosuvastatin to cause rhabdomyolysis.

The PRAC applied both conclusions to *every* product containing rosuvastatin, not just the combination. Both now appear in the Crestor SmPC: the severe skin reaction warning in section 4.4, and ticagrelor (×2.6 exposure) in section 4.5.

## A class-wide **signal**

A signal is new information suggesting that a medicine may cause an effect, strong enough to need checking.

In January 2023 the PRAC concluded that all statins, and every combination product containing one, should warn about myasthenia gravis and ocular myasthenia. These conditions can appear for the first time or get worse, with frequency not known. Treatment should stop if symptoms worsen, and symptoms have come back when the same or a different statin was restarted.

The Crestor SmPC and PIL now carry this warning.

## Safety decisions from the early years

Rosuvastatin's early safety history set limits that are still in place today:

- The 80 mg dose was withdrawn.
- 40 mg was restricted to severe cases under specialist supervision.
- Asian patients were given a lower starting dose.
- Kidney function checks were recommended at 40 mg.

The company has kept a **risk management plan** (RMP), a document listing a medicine's risks and how each one is managed and studied, since at least 2009. No public RMP summary for Crestor was found in this pass.

## The watchlist

Two items sit outside the label for now:

- **Cataract.** LODESTAR and HOPE-3 both reported more cataract surgery on rosuvastatin. The SmPC doesn't mention cataract, and no PRAC assessment of it was found in this pass.
- **A leaflet-only line.** The PIL warns about severe respiratory insufficiency, but there is no matching line in the SmPC (Lesson 12).

Neither is proof of anything. Both are the kind of item that a regular review is designed to catch.

## What triggers a refresh of this module

- A new revision of the Crestor SmPC
- A PSUSA for rosuvastatin, or for a rosuvastatin combination, that ends with a variation
- A PRAC signal on statins or on rosuvastatin

The current basis is the October 2025 SmPC. The next scheduled refresh is March 2027.

lessons.title: Where the ESC guidelines place it

blocks.markdown:
## Guidelines, not licences

The ESC/EAS guidelines advise on practice. They don't change what a product is licensed for.

Each recommendation carries a **class of recommendation**: I means 'is recommended', IIa 'should be considered', IIb 'may be considered' and III 'is not recommended'. It also carries a **level of evidence**, from A (several randomised trials) to C (expert consensus or small studies).

## 2019: statins at the centre

The 2019 guidelines set LDL goals by risk level:

- Very-high risk: at least a 50% reduction and LDL below 1.4 mmol/L. This is I A for secondary prevention and I C for primary prevention.
- High risk: at least a 50% reduction and LDL below 1.8 mmol/L (I A).

The drug steps are:

1. A **high-intensity statin**, one that lowers LDL by about half, up to the highest tolerated dose (I A).
2. Add ezetimibe if the goal isn't reached (I B).
3. Add a PCSK9 inhibitor in very-high-risk secondary prevention if the goal still isn't reached (I A).

For raised triglycerides in high-risk people, a statin is the first choice (I B).

## Where rosuvastatin fits

The guidelines talk about statin intensity, not brands. The RACING investigators describe rosuvastatin 10 mg as moderate intensity and 20 mg as high intensity.

This creates a tension worth noticing. The guideline says to go up to the highest *tolerated* dose. The EU label reserves 40 mg for severe high cholesterol at high risk that isn't at goal on 20 mg, starts it under specialist supervision, and contraindicates it in several groups (Lesson 12). The label sets the outer limits that the guideline's advice has to work within.

## 2025: the focused update

The 2025 update left the LDL goals unchanged and moved risk estimation to SCORE2 and SCORE2-OP. For rosuvastatin, the changes that matter are:

- Acute coronary syndrome: intensify existing lipid treatment in hospital (I C). In people not already on treatment who are unlikely to reach the goal on a statin alone, start a high-intensity statin *plus ezetimibe* during that hospital stay (IIa B).
- Statin intolerance: non-statin medicines with proven cardiovascular benefit, such as ezetimibe, are recommended (I A), and bempedoic acid is named specifically (I B).
- Bempedoic acid may be added when the goal isn't reached on the maximum tolerated statin, with or without ezetimibe (IIa C).

## A practical consequence

The 2025 update suggests starting a statin and ezetimibe *together* after an acute coronary syndrome. The Spanish rosuvastatin/ezetimibe combination tablets, however, are labelled as not suitable for starting treatment.

Following the guideline within those licences means starting with separate tablets and switching to the combination tablet once the doses are settled. The guideline and the label don't contradict each other; they operate at different levels.

## Rosuvastatin on one page

*Basis: Crestor 5/10/20 mg SmPC (Spain), October 2025 revision. Next refresh: March 2027.*

**What it is.** A statin that blocks HMG-CoA reductase in the liver. The liver responds by making more LDL receptors, which pull LDL out of the blood. Most of its interactions work through transporters (OATP1B1, BCRP), not liver enzymes.

**What it's approved for.** High cholesterol and mixed dyslipidaemia from age 6; homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia from age 6; and prevention of a first cardiovascular event in high-risk people. That last indication is drawn from JUPITER's post-hoc higher-risk analyses.

**How it's taken.** Once a day, at any time, with or without food. Start at 5 or 10 mg, or 5 mg if over 70, of Asian origin, with moderate kidney impairment or with interacting medicines. The dose can be stepped up after 4 weeks. 40 mg is restricted and started under a specialist.

**What it does to events.**
- JUPITER vs placebo (median 1.9 years, stopped early): HR 0.56; about 6 fewer events per 1,000 people per year.
- HOPE-3 vs placebo (5.6 years): 3.7% vs 4.8%, HR 0.76.
- Heart failure (CORONA) and dialysis (AURORA): no benefit.
- Against atorvastatin (LODESTAR): similar outcomes.

**Combinations.** Spanish substitution tablets pair it with ezetimibe, fenofibrate, amlodipine, valsartan or aspirin. RACING found rosuvastatin 10 mg plus ezetimibe no worse than 20 mg alone. HOPE-3's combined arm with candesartan and hydrochlorothiazide gave HR 0.71. Most of the other blood-pressure combination trials are 8-week studies of blood pressure and LDL only.

**Safety.** Muscle aches are common and rhabdomyolysis rare. Protein in the urine appears at 40 mg. There is a diabetes signal (JUPITER, LODESTAR), and cataract appears in trials but not in the label. DRESS and myasthenia warnings came from EU safety reviews. Fusidic acid and ciclosporin are the key interactions to avoid.

**Guidelines.** High-intensity statin, then ezetimibe, then a PCSK9 inhibitor. From 2025, statin plus ezetimibe can be started together after an acute coronary syndrome.

options: Ticagrelor raises rosuvastatin exposure about 2.6-fold, and the combination has been linked to rhabdomyolysis, so benefit and risk need weighing
questions.explanation: The SmPC lists ticagrelor at ×2.6 exposure, and the PRAC established the interaction as a cause of rhabdomyolysis. Weigh the benefits of both medicines against the higher exposure.

questions.stem: Which finding appears in rosuvastatin trials but not in the Crestor SmPC?
options: Protein in the urine at 40 mg
questions.explanation: Rhabdomyolysis, diabetes and proteinuria are all in the SmPC. Cataract surgery was more frequent on rosuvastatin in LODESTAR and HOPE-3, but the label doesn't mention it (Lessons 11 and 13).
